resume:
Languages : C++, Golang, SQL, Javascript, HTML, CSS
Frameworks : React , Node.js, Express.js, React-Native, Expo
Developer Tools : Docker, VS Code, GoLand, Android Studio, Firebase, TablePlus, Postman, GitHub, Bitbucket, Jira
Databases/Caching : PostgreSQL, Redis, PgAdmin 4, Medis
Cloud/Devops : AWS(CloudWatch, ElastiCache, ECS, API Gateway), Grafana, BitBucket Pipelines, Mixpanel
Development Practices : Clean Architecture, SOLID Principles, Interface-Based Design, Dependency Injection,
Test-Driven Development (TDD), Error Handling & Logging
Experience
AppsForBharat | Golang, React, Docker, Postgres, Redis, AWS, Grafana, Mixpanel May 2025 – Present
Software Developer Bangalore, India
• Built and scaled Golang microservices for Puja, Chadhava, Astrology, Wallet, and Temple domains, serving
10M+ global users; designed RESTful APIs with PostgreSQL, Redis caching, async workers, and clean
architecture to ensure high availability and low latency.
• Architected and owned a scalable Content Management System (CMS) for pre-order operations,
implementing fine-grained RBAC and optimized maker–checker workflows; simplified approval flows, reduced ops
turnaround time, improved analytics visibility, and integrated LLM automation.
• Optimized backend performance and developer productivity by enhancing Redis caching strategies,
concurrency-safe shared utilities, and CI/CD pipelines; achieved 40% faster data access, improved
deployment reliability, and increased automated test coverage to 90%.
• Improved LLM-driven systems by optimizing prompt flows for Dify-based chatbots, reducing response latency
and improving answer quality; deployed and monitored services using AWS (ECS, AppConfig, CloudWatch)
and Grafana for metrics, logging, and performance analysis.

last_question: Hey, thanks so much for coming in — really glad to have you here. Let's start easy. Just give me a quick intro about yourself — who you are, what you've been up to lately, whatever feels natural.

active_question_packet.question_text: Hey, thanks so much for coming in — really glad to have you here. Let's start easy. Just give me a quick intro about yourself — who you are, what you've been up to lately, whatever feels natural.

focus_areas.label: Golang Microservices Platform For High-Scale Religious Commerce
focus_areas.anchor_context: Built and scaled Golang microservices across Puja, Chadhava, Astrology, Wallet, and Temple domains serving 10M+ global users with Redis, PostgreSQL, and async workers.
sub_focuses: RESTful API design with PostgreSQL and Redis caching under high load
async worker architecture and concurrency-safe shared utilities
40% faster data access claim and how it was measured
CI/CD pipeline improvements and 90% automated test coverage methodology
resume_snippets: Built and scaled Golang microservices for Puja, Chadhava, Astrology, Wallet, and Temple domains, serving 10M+ global users
achieved 40% faster data access, improved deployment reliability, and increased automated test coverage to 90%
focus_areas.why_priority: Candidate claims end-to-end ownership of microservices at 10M-user scale with specific latency and coverage metrics that
focus_areas.opener: At AppsForBharat, you built Golang microservices across five domains for 10M+ users — what was the hardest architectural problem you hit when those domains had to share state or communicate?

dimensions.label: RESTful API Design with Redis and PostgreSQL Under High Load
dimensions.resume_anchor: designed RESTful APIs with PostgreSQL, Redis caching, async workers, and clean architecture to ensure high availability and low latency
dimensions.surface: In the Wallet or Chadhava service, what data did you choose to cache in Redis versus always read from PostgreSQL, and why?
dimensions.mechanism: When a Redis cache entry for a Puja or Temple resource becomes stale mid-request, how does your API layer handle that — and what consistency guarantees does that give you?
dimensions.boundary: At 10M users, what specific failure mode in your Redis-PostgreSQL interaction did you have to design around — something that only showed up under actual concurrent write pressure?

dimensions.label: Async Worker Architecture and Concurrency-Safe Utilities
dimensions.resume_anchor: concurrency-safe shared utilities, and async workers
dimensions.surface: In the Astrology or Puja domain, what work did you offload to async workers, and what triggered them?
dimensions.mechanism: What made a shared utility in your Golang codebase unsafe for concurrent use, and what specific change did you make to fix that across the microservices that shared it?
dimensions.boundary: If an async worker for a Wallet transaction fails halfway through, what state does your system leave behind — and how did you discover that edge case rather than assume it was handled?

dimensions.label: 40% Faster Data Access — Measurement and Validity
dimensions.surface: What specific operation or query type did the 40% faster data access figure apply to — which domain and which endpoint?
dimensions.mechanism: How did you isolate the Redis caching improvement as the cause of that 40% gain rather than any other change deployed around the same time?
dimensions.boundary: What was your baseline measurement — what tool captured it, what load level was it taken at, and how did you ensure the before and after conditions were comparable?

dimensions.label: CI/CD Pipeline Improvements and 90% Test Coverage Methodology
dimensions.resume_anchor: improved deployment reliability, and increased automated test coverage to 90%
dimensions.surface: In your Bitbucket Pipelines setup, what does a failed pipeline stage actually block — does it stop deployment, or does it alert and continue?
dimensions.mechanism: Your test coverage went to 90% — what was excluded from that 90%, and was that a deliberate call or a gap you accepted?
dimensions.boundary: In the Golang microservices, how did you write tests for code paths that depend on Redis or PostgreSQL without making those tests slow or brittle — what specifically did you mock or stub, and what did you not?

dimensions.label: Microservice Domain Boundaries Across Puja, Wallet, Astrology
dimensions.resume_anchor: Built and scaled Golang microservices for Puja, Chadhava, Astrology, Wallet, and Temple domains, serving 10M+ global users
dimensions.surface: When the Wallet domain needs data that lives in the Temple or Puja domain, how does it get it — direct DB access, internal API call, or something else?
dimensions.mechanism: What happens to in-flight Wallet transactions if the Puja service goes down — how does your architecture prevent that cascade from propagating?
dimensions.boundary: Across five domains at this user scale, what was the hardest ownership or data consistency problem you personally had to resolve — something that required a decision no clean architecture pattern gave you directly?

recovery.short_answer: You mentioned Redis caching in the Wallet or Puja service — pick one endpoint and tell me exactly what you cached, what the key structure looked like, and what the TTL was.
recovery.honest_gap: That's fair — tell me the part of this platform you do understand at the implementation level, whether that's the caching layer, the async workers, or the test setup.
recovery.claim_conflict: Your resume says you designed RESTful APIs for high availability across five domains, but your answer describes a single service in isolation — how did your design account for the other domains depending on that service being up?
recovery.metric_risk: You cited 40% faster data access — before I move on, I need to understand the denominator: 40% of what, measured how, at what request volume, and compared to what baseline state?
recovery.overclaim_risk: You used the term 'concurrency-safe' — in your specific Golang code, what does that mean concretely: a mutex, a channel, an atomic operation, or something else, and on which shared resource exactly?
recovery.bridge: Got it — let's move to the other major system you owned at AppsForBharat. You architected the RBAC-gated CMS with LLM automation and maker-checker workflows for pre-order operations. I want to understand how you designed the permission boundaries and where the LLM fit into that approval flow.

candidate_q4_options: In your Golang microservices, how did clean architecture and dependency injection interact — what did that actually look like in a domain like Astrology or Wallet where external dependencies were involved?
Grafana and CloudWatch were both in your stack — for the same service, when did you reach for one over the other, and what gap did each leave?
Across Puja, Chadhava, and Temple domains serving 10M users, how did you handle schema migrations in PostgreSQL without taking a service down?
The Wallet domain in a high-scale religious commerce platform has real-money risk — what constraints did that put on your API design or error handling that the other domains did not have?

focus_areas.label: Rbac-Gated Cms With LLM Automation And Maker-Checker Workflows
focus_areas.anchor_context: Architected a scalable CMS for pre-order operations with fine-grained RBAC, maker-checker approval flows, and integrated LLM automation via Dify-based chatbots.
sub_focuses: fine-grained RBAC schema design and enforcement at the API layer
maker-checker workflow implementation and approval state machine
LLM prompt optimization for Dify chatbots and latency/quality tradeoffs
AWS ECS and AppConfig deployment with CloudWatch and Grafana observability
resume_snippets: Architected and owned a scalable Content Management System (CMS) for pre-order operations, implementing fine-grained RBAC and optimized maker-checker workflows
focus_areas.why_priority: Candidate claims full ownership of a multi-surface system combining access control design, workflow state management, an
focus_areas.opener: At AppsForBharat, you architected the CMS for pre-order operations — what was the core problem that made a custom CMS necessary instead of an off-the-shelf solution?

dimensions.label: Fine-Grained RBAC Design and API Enforcement
dimensions.resume_anchor: implementing fine-grained RBAC and optimized maker-checker workflows
dimensions.surface: In the CMS RBAC model, how did you represent permissions — were they role-level, resource-level, or action-level, and what drove that choice?
dimensions.mechanism: Fine-grained RBAC implies permissions below the role level — at the API layer in your CMS, how did enforcement happen without repeating that logic across every handler?
dimensions.boundary: In your CMS, what happens when a user's role changes mid-session — how does your enforcement layer handle the permission state without requiring a full logout?

dimensions.label: Maker-Checker Approval State Machine
dimensions.resume_anchor: optimized maker-checker workflows; simplified approval flows, reduced ops turnaround time
dimensions.surface: In the maker-checker flow you built, what are the distinct states a pre-order record can be in, and what triggers each transition?
dimensions.mechanism: When a checker rejects a record in your approval flow, what happens to the maker's original payload — is it preserved, discarded, or versioned, and why did you design it that way?
dimensions.boundary: In your maker-checker implementation, what prevents a maker from approving their own record if they also hold a checker role — and where exactly in the system does that constraint live?

dimensions.label: LLM Prompt Optimization and Latency/Quality Tradeoffs
dimensions.resume_anchor: integrated LLM automation; optimizing prompt flows for Dify-based chatbots, reducing response latency and improving answer quality
dimensions.surface: In the Dify-based chatbot integration, what specifically did you change in the prompt flow to reduce latency — was it prompt length, model selection, chaining structure, or something else?
dimensions.mechanism: Reducing latency and improving answer quality are often in tension in LLM systems — in your Dify flows for the CMS, where did you land on that tradeoff and what data drove that decision?
dimensions.boundary: In your Dify integration, how do you detect when a prompt flow produces a degraded answer in production — what does a bad output look like and what triggers a review or rollback?

dimensions.label: AWS ECS, AppConfig, and Grafana Observability
dimensions.resume_anchor: deployed and monitored services using AWS (ECS, AppConfig, CloudWatch) and Grafana for metrics, logging, and performance analysis
dimensions.surface: For the CMS services running on ECS, how did you use AppConfig — was it for feature flags, environment-specific config, or something else in the pre-order context?
dimensions.mechanism: In your Grafana setup for these services, what specific metrics did you instrument to catch a performance regression before it affected the 10M+ user base?
dimensions.boundary: In your ECS deployment for the CMS, what does a failed deployment look like in CloudWatch, and what's the exact recovery path — do you roll back the task definition, the config, or both?

recovery.short_answer: You mentioned the RBAC implementation — name one specific database table or middleware component you wrote for it and describe exactly what it does.
recovery.honest_gap: That's fair — which part of this system do you have the clearest ownership of, RBAC enforcement, the approval state machine, or the Dify integration? Start there.
recovery.claim_conflict: You said you architected and owned this CMS, but your answer describes something more like implementation of a spec — who actually made the design decisions on the RBAC schema and approval states?
recovery.metric_risk: You mentioned reduced ops turnaround time — what was the unit of measurement, what was the before number, and how was it captured — manual timing, logs, or something instrumented?
recovery.overclaim_risk: You used the term fine-grained RBAC — in your specific implementation, what is the smallest unit of permission, what schema stores it, and give me one example of a permission that a coarser role-based model couldn't express.
recovery.bridge: That covers the CMS architecture well — let's move to the Golang Microservices Platform For High-Scale Religious Commerce, specifically how the Puja, Wallet, and Temple services are structured and how they handle load at 10M+ users.

candidate_q4_options: In the CMS RBAC model, how did you handle a scenario where two roles have conflicting permissions on the same resource — which permission wins and where is that rule enforced?
The maker-checker flow reduced ops turnaround time — how did you measure turnaround time before and after, and what was the baseline you were comparing against?
In your Dify chatbot integration with the CMS, what triggers the LLM path versus a deterministic code path — and how did you decide where that boundary sits?
You own the CMS end-to-end — if a checker approves a record that later fails downstream in the pre-order pipeline, what does your system do with that approved state?

strengths: Boundary probes throughout are genuinely hands-on — 'what state does your system leave behind', 'what prevents a maker from approving their own record', and 'what was your baseline measurement' all require real ownership to answer correctly.

Signal-weight 3.0 dimensions are correctly prioritized on the highest-risk resume claims (40% data access, RBAC design, concurrency-safe utilities), and the metric_risk recovery for both areas is precise and targeted.
The recovery overlays are complete and well-differentiated — each of the five recovery types maps to a distinct failure mode specific to this candidate's claims.
issues: Both openers invite narrative rather than forcing an immediate analytical position. 'What was the hardest architectural problem' and 'what was the core problem that made a custom CMS necessary' are open-ended reflections, not causal challenges — a strong candidate can answer both with a polished story without revealing depth.

Focus area 1, dimension 'ci_cd_test_coverage' (signal_weight 2.0): the surface probe ('does a failed pipeline stage stop deployment or alert and continue') is answerable from reading the Bitbucket Pipelines documentation — it doesn't require having owned this pipeline.

Focus area 2, dimension 'aws_ecs_appconfig_observability' (signal_weight 2.0): the surface probe on AppConfig usage is generic infrastructure trivia — any developer who configured AppConfig once could answer it without having owned this CMS deployment.
repair_instructions: Opener fix for focus area 1: Replace 'what was the hardest architectural problem' with a direct causal challenge anchored to a specific claim: 'Your Wallet service shares infrastructure with Puja and Astrology domains at 10M users — when you added Redis caching, what data consistency problem did that create between the Wallet and one of those other domains, and how did you resolve it?' This forces an immediate technical position rather than a retrospective narrative.

Opener fix for focus area 2: Replace 'what was the core problem that made a custom CMS necessary' with a hypothesis challenge: 'You implemented fine-grained RBAC over a maker-checker workflow — those two systems have overlapping authorization logic. Where exactly did they conflict in your design, and which one took precedence?' This anchors to a real design tension rather than inviting a product justification story.

Repair ci_cd_test_coverage surface probe: Replace 'does a failed pipeline stage stop deployment or alert and continue' with 'In your Bitbucket Pipeline for these microservices, what specific test or check was the last thing added before you hit 90% coverage — and what category of code did it cover that you hadn't tested before?' This requires actual authorship of the pipeline, not documentation familiarity.

Repair aws_ecs_appconfig_observability surface probe: Replace the generic AppConfig question with 'In your ECS deployment for the CMS, which Grafana dashboard metric first told you a pre-order operation was degraded — name the metric, what it measures, and what threshold you set for an alert.' This requires having instrumented the service, not just having used AppConfig.
